title: Meta defends AI glasses in court as Dutch groups demand ban
content:
Meta defends AI glasses in court as Dutch groups demand ban
Meta has argued that it cannot be held liable for the misuse of its AI-powered smart glasses. Lawyers for the U.S. tech company made the case during a hearing at the Amsterdam District Court, where several organizations are seeking a ban on the product.
The three Dutch organizations told the Amsterdam court that Meta's camera glasses pose a threat to democratic society and should be banned. The devices allow wearers to secretly record video and audio, the groups argued. Their lawyer accused Meta of "normalizing mass surveillance with its peeping glasses."
Meta argued that any product can be misused by someone intent on doing so, adding that it has measures in place to prevent abuse. The company's lawyers also said banning its glasses would not address the issue, as other manufacturers sell similar camera-equipped eyewear.
The Dutch Consumers' Association, online safety organization Offlimits and advocacy group The Firewall brought the case, citing concerns about people's privacy. They called the technology a "danger to democratic society."
Meta said banning the glasses would unfairly affect the vast majority of customers who use them legitimately and have no intention of misusing the technology.
The glasses are designed to resemble regular eyewear, but a small light on the front flashes when the wearer records a video. Meta said research had identified this as the most effective way to alert people that they are being filmed. The company added that the device takes action if someone attempts to cover the indicator light.
The organizations have also raised concerns about the data Meta collects through the glasses. The company says it does not use photos and videos captured with the device to train its AI systems. However, if users choose to share that content publicly on Meta's platforms, the company can use it for AI training, just as it does with other publicly shared material.
The organizations accuse Meta of breaching regulations, particularly those protecting people's privacy. Their lawyer said many people had been recorded without their consent or even knowing it was happening. "Our democratic society is at stake if everyone has to fear being filmed at all times," the lawyer said.
Offlimits and The Firewall argue that banning the AI-powered glasses is the only effective solution. They said financial penalties or settlements would not change Meta's conduct, accusing the company of making money by failing to comply with the law. "Not complying with the law is its business model," they said.
The Consumers' Association is not explicitly demanding that the glasses be banned. Instead, it wants Meta to introduce "appropriate measures" to prevent covert recording and to stop using data collected through the device to train its AI systems.
The concerns have also been raised by other organizations and regulators, including the Dutch Data Protection Authority. Optical retailer Hans Anders stopped selling Meta's smart glasses last month, with no set date for resuming sales.
The organizations also reject Meta's arguments about the glasses being useful for people with visual impairments. "If that is the argument, then the glasses should also be restricted to that group. Moreover, the glasses do not comply with the applicable laws and regulations even when used by people with visual impairments," the opponents of the product said.
The court is expected to deliver its ruling no later than December 24.
Reporting by ANP

report.summary: Meta told an Amsterdam court it is not liable for misuse of its AI glasses, as Dutch privacy groups seek a ban over covert recording.
report.background: AI-powered camera glasses have revived privacy debates that began with Google Glass a decade ago. The current generation, including Meta's Ray-Ban smart glasses, packs cameras, microphones, and AI assistants into everyday frames. Supporters see hands-free computing and accessibility benefits; critics see covert recording and mass surveillance. In Europe, GDPR and national privacy rules require clear legal bases, transparency, and data minimization. Dutch regulators and consumer groups have become increasingly assertive about wearable cameras and platform data practices. The Amsterdam case tests whether product liability, privacy law, or a sales ban is the right response to dual-use hardware. It also comes as AI features make it easier to analyze captured audio and video, raising the stakes for bystanders who may never consent. The outcome could influence how wearables are designed and sold across the EU.
key_points: The hearing at Amsterdam District Court pits three Dutch organizations—the Consumers' Association, Offlimits, and The Firewall—against Meta. They argue the glasses enable secret video and audio recording and normalize mass surveillance. Two groups want a ban; the Consumers' Association seeks measures to prevent covert recording and stop AI training on device data.

Meta's defense is that any product can be misused and a ban would punish legitimate users while not solving the problem because rival camera glasses exist. It points to a recording indicator light and says the device reacts if someone covers it. Meta also says banning its product would unfairly affect customers with no intent to misuse it.

Data practices are central. Meta says it does not use photos or videos captured with the glasses to train its AI unless users publicly share that content on Meta platforms, in which case it may be used like other public material. The groups say many people have been recorded without consent or knowledge.

The case reflects broader scrutiny. The Dutch Data Protection Authority has raised concerns, and optical retailer Hans Anders stopped selling Meta's smart glasses last month with no restart date. The organizations reject accessibility arguments, saying if visual impairment were the rationale, sales should be restricted to that group and the product still must comply with law.

The court is expected to rule by December 24. Possible outcomes include rejecting the ban, ordering specific safeguards, or requiring changes to data use. The decision will be an early European test of how courts treat dual-use AI wearables and whether product bans are proportionate remedies for privacy harms.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the case is a precedent-setting stress test: camera-equipped wearables may face jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction legal risk, pushing companies toward privacy-by-design, stronger consent flows, on-device processing, and clear recording indicators. Developers building vision or audio AI should assume stricter scrutiny of bystander consent and training data provenance; 'publicly posted' is not a blanket license. Regular users could see more prominent recording warnings, feature limits, or delayed launches in privacy-sensitive markets. A ban would be a strong signal that dual-use hardware can be restricted when safeguards are deemed insufficient; a narrow ruling could instead entrench LED indicators and terms-of-service as the compliance model. Either way, expect more litigation and regulatory attention across the EU.
report.tools: To follow privacy-preserving wearable AI, watch OpenGlass, an open-source smart-glasses project, and MediaPipe/TensorFlow Lite for on-device vision and audio processing that can reduce cloud data exposure. OpenCV is useful for prototyping camera pipelines and recording-indicator detection. For compliance, review GDPR data-protection impact assessment (DPIA) templates from CNIL or the Dutch DPA, and follow Offlimits and The Firewall's publications for the case. These are not legal advice but practical starting points.
